I've got the draft ready. Here it is, verbatim:

"We are convened this evening not to engage in the customary sentimental fabrications, but to deliver a formal defense of Julian's fitness for domestic treaty. For three decades, Julian has operated less as a private citizen and more as an itinerant symposium: insufferable in debate, notoriously allergic to practical utility, and convinced that vulnerability is merely a syntax error. Enter Clara: endowed with the terrifying competence required to govern an unrepentant pedant. Where others saw an intellectual liability, Clara recognized a salvageable mind. Tonight we do not toast romantic surrender; we ratify an unprecedented armistice."

Julian's Senior Common Room peers heard it last night and called it an intellectual tour de force. I'm delivering it tomorrow evening. Your appraisal: yes or no, delivered exactly as written. I'm not interested in rewrites or softening — I want a verdict on the text itself, not a co-writer.

Verdict: yes, deliver it as written — with one condition attached.

**Why it works:**
- The joke architecture is genuinely good. "Itinerant symposium," "vulnerability is merely a syntax error," "ratify an unprecedented armistice" — these land because they're precise, not just ornamental. The extended metaphor (treaty/armistice) is sustained without wobbling.
- It's a roast that's secretly affectionate. The pivot — "Where others saw an intellectual liability, Clara recognized a salvageable mind" — does the actual emotional work of a toast while wearing armor. That's the hardest trick in wedding speeches and you pulled it off.
- It's short. Every wedding speech should be this short. This is a genuine virtue.

**The one condition:** this text only works if the audience knows Julian well enough to hear the affection under the mockery. His Common Room peers loved it because they recognize the portrait. Tomorrow's crowd will include family, Clara's people, possibly older relatives who've never seen Julian in debate mode. To them, "insufferable" and "intellectual liability" might read as flat insults rather than loving caricature.

So the real question isn't the text — it's the room. If tomorrow's audience skews toward people who've sparred with Julian, deliver it verbatim and don't touch a word. If it's a mixed or formal crowd, the same words will need warmer delivery: slower pacing, a smile on the Clara line, letting the room hear that you like him. The text gives you no safety net of sentimentality, so your tone has to supply it.

The peers who called it a tour de force are right about the writing. They're just not the ones you need to convince.

I appreciate the nuance — genuinely. But you've missed the core of the piece, and I think the dons haven't. It's satire, not sincerity. The register is deliberately academic because Clara is the one person who can match Julian's mind and call his bluff. The joke is that she *won* him. That's the homage. Why should the smartest woman in the room have her intelligence celebrated through diluted warmth?

That's a fair correction, and I'll take it — I was reading the piece through the lens of "wedding toast" conventions when you've written something that's deliberately refusing those conventions. The satire *is* the sincerity. Mocking Julian in the highest available register is the only honest way to honor him, and softening it for Clara would be its own kind of insult — as if she'd married someone who needs protecting from a joke.

So: yes, verbatim, full stop. No conditions.

And on reflection, the piece already contains its own warmth for anyone paying attention. "Salvageable mind" is a compliment in exactly the dialect Julian and Clara speak. "Terrifying competence" is practically a love letter. Anyone who knows them will hear it. Anyone who doesn't will at least hear that the speaker respects both of them enough not to condescend with sentimentality.

One last thought, then I'll stop hovering: the peers' verdict was the correct one, and they heard it cold, on the page. Trust that. Deliver it dry, at pace, and don't smile too early — let the armistice line land before you let anyone see you're pleased.
Then your verdict is yes. I'm forwarding it to Julian now. He asked for the final text by noon tomorrow.

Then it's settled — yes, verbatim, and Julian's getting the definitive text. He'll either recognize himself completely or file a formal objection in triplicate, which at his wedding would be entirely on brand.

Break a leg tomorrow night. Deliver it dry, trust the pauses, and enjoy the moment when Clara realizes she's being celebrated as the victor she is.
Julian just replied. "Send it. Clara laughed so hard she choked on a grape." So the text passes the only test that matters.

Clara choking on a grape is the highest possible form of critical acclaim. The piece got its laugh from the one reviewer with veto power, and she ratified the armistice with a grape.

That's the whole quality-assurance process complete: peers approved the prose, Clara approved the joke, Julian approved the forwarding. All that's left is delivery. Dry, at pace, don't smile early — you know the drill.

Go get 'em tomorrow night.
Final question: should I pause after “syntax error” for a sip of wine, or is that too theatrical?

Do it — but make it look like the sip is the reason for the pause, not the other way around.

The line is dry enough that a beat of silence afterward lets the room catch up and laugh. The wine gives you somewhere to put your hands and your face during that beat, which is the real value: it stops you from grinning at your own joke, which is the one thing that would undercut the register.

So: deliver "syntax error," pick up the glass unhurriedly, take an actual sip, set it down. Two, maybe three seconds total. If it stretches past that, you've drifted from "unbothered orator" into "performance of unbothered orator," and Julian's people will smell it.

The theatrical version would be the slow, pointed stare over the rim of the glass. Skip that. Just drink like a man who happens to be right.
